title: Energy security in the age of AI | Wood Mackenzie
gist: On Wood Mackenzie's Energy Gang podcast at ADIPEC 2026, AVEVA CEO Caspar Herzberg argues energy security now hinges on whole-system data visibility (a 'living digital twin'), physically secured digital infrastructure, and a mix of micro grids and continent-scale macro grids. He contends large AI data centers must become net contributors to grid stability, since their impact on reliability and household costs depends on design and operation.

insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Signals demand for cross-supply-chain industrial software as a security spend category, not just efficiency.

insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Resilience framing gives Schneider Electric's software arm a geopolitical-risk tailwind narrative.

insights.so_what: Value in industrial data shifts from collection/storage toward decision-support and analytics layers.

insights.claim: Data centers and subsea cables are increasingly potential targets, making digital infrastructure part of the energy security question.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Raises the case for physical/cyber hardening spend and redundancy in digital infrastructure.
insights.quote: Data centers and subsea cables can become targets.

insights.claim: Threats to digital infrastructure are prompting a rethink of where critical data lives, shifting some from global cloud services toward regional and on-premises systems, alongside demand for more redundancy and regulation.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Implies a sovereign/regional and on-prem data hosting tailwind at the margin versus pure hyperscale cloud.
insights.quote: prompting a rethink of where critical data lives, from global cloud services to regional and on-premises systems

insights.claim: A resilient system requires investment both in distributed micro grids and in large-scale macro grids that are 'bigger than the weather', with larger grids balancing weather-driven output across regions while distributed renewables make supply harder to disrupt.

insights.so_what: Supports a dual capex thesis: interregional transmission and distributed generation/storage both benefit.

insights.so_what: Policy stability is flagged as the binding constraint for grid and interconnector investment returns.

themes.theme: AI data centers and the grid

insights.claim: Herzberg says large data centers will increasingly have to be net contributors to grid stability, planned as industrial sites with better workload visibility, optimized cooling and flexibility that does not compromise reliability.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Points to coming requirements for data-center flexibility, favoring operators and vendors that can offer grid services.
insights.quote: Increasingly, large data centers are going to have to be net contributors to the stability of the grid

insights.claim: AI-driven power demand cuts both ways: it can strain reliability and raise household power costs, or support the grid and help hold costs down by providing additional flexibility, depending critically on how new large data centers are designed and operated.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Affordability backlash risk for AI load is real; design/operation choices will shape regulatory treatment and interconnection terms.
insights.quote: The impact of new large data centers will depend critically on how they are designed and operated.
